facts.title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
facts.event_hint: An empirical comparison of Semantic Search (prebuilt vector-index retrieval) versus Deep Agentic Search (planner delegating exploration to an isolated subagent, a.k.a. grep-search by subagent) on the SWE-QA repo-level code-QA benchmark; Semantic search is more accurate and cheaper, while Deep Agentic search introduces a new hand-off failure class.
facts.problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating the right code in a repository, and the choice between index-based Semantic Search and hierarchical Deep Agentic Search (used to protect the main agent from context rot / context pollution) has direct consequences for accuracy, cost, and latency. Recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) adopted Deep Agentic Search quickly, but the two paradigms had not been empirically compared for repository-level code question answering, so the debate rests largely on intuition.
facts.mechanism: Two agent architectures are compared on SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a) across four language models. The Semantic side is a flat ReAct agent (LangChain ReAct harness) restricted to three tools: a repository-structure lookup, a retrieval tool over a vector index built once per repo (file chunking + embedding + similarity retrieval), and a file reader. The Deep Agentic side is a hierarchical Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework, default toolset: planning, a virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation). Each question runs in a fresh conversation thread with only the target repository available; all tool calls, planner steps, sub-agent actions, and token counts are recorded. Answers are graded by an LLM judge validated against an independent human panel. The authors argue the two action spaces cannot be made identical because the tool difference is intrinsic to each paradigm rather than a confound.

evidence.claim: Semantic search answers 65.2% of questions correctly versus 46.2% for Deep Agentic search (pooled across the four model conditions, matching the mean of the per-model Pass rates in Table 3). The within-model Pass-rate difference favours Semantic by 5.6pp (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 10.0pp (Gemini 2.5 Pro), 10.6pp (Qwen3-235B), and 49.6pp (Gemini 3 Flash); all four McNemar and all four Wilcoxon tests remain significant after false discovery rate correction.
evidence.value: 65.2% vs 46.2% (pooled); +5.6 to +49.6pp Semantic advantage per model
evidence.baseline: Deep Agentic search within the same model and benchmark
evidence.condition: SWE-QA benchmark, four LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B); Cliff's delta ~0.14 for the Gemini 2.5 pair, 0.24 for Qwen3-235B, 0.76 for Gemini 3 Flash (effect modest for Gemini 2.5, large only for Gemini 3 Flash)
evidence.source_locator: Abstract PDF Page 1; Table 3 and paired within-model comparison, PDF Page 15

evidence.claim: Semantic search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of Deep Agentic search. Per-model dollars-per-Pass: Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.213 vs 0.436; Gemini 2.5 Pro 1.048 vs 1.526; Gemini 3 Flash 0.179 vs 0.858; Qwen3-235B 0.012 vs 0.291.
evidence.value: $/Pass roughly 2x cheaper for Semantic across all four models
evidence.baseline: Deep Agentic search $/Pass within the same model
evidence.condition: Cost includes reasoning tokens billed at completion rate (so cost is not the simple product of the in/out token columns and list prices); token columns count prompt+completion tokens only
evidence.source_locator: Abstract PDF Page 1; Table 3, PDF Page 15

evidence.claim: A six-mechanism failure taxonomy shows Deep Agentic search did not eliminate failures but introduced a new class: the single largest share of Deep failures, 41.8%, were coordination breakdowns at the planner-to-sub-agent hand-off, and 0% for Semantic (a flat retrieval agent has no such hand-off). The association between architecture and failure mechanism is very strong: chi-square 508.8 on 5 df, Cramer's V 0.56; restricted to the five mechanisms available to both architectures the association remains large (chi-square 147.2 on 4 df, V 0.35).
evidence.value: 41.8% of Deep failures are coordination breakdowns; 0% for Semantic
evidence.baseline: Semantic-search failure distribution over the same taxonomy
evidence.condition: Coded from recorded execution traces; hand-off failures usually silent, ending in a fluent confident wrong answer
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.3 / Figure 19, PDF Page 26; restated in Abstract PDF Page 1

evidence.claim: Despite higher cost and lower accuracy, Deep Agentic search has lower median latency for three of four models: Gemini 2.5 Flash 106s vs 329s (Semantic), Gemini 2.5 Pro 152s vs 400s, Qwen3-235B 105s vs 42s (here Deep is slower), and Gemini 3 Flash 262s vs 101s (Deep slower). The latency trade-off is therefore model-dependent and does not consistently favour either paradigm.
evidence.value: Median latency per question from Table 3 (model-dependent)
evidence.baseline: Semantic search median latency within the same model
evidence.condition: Single-question fresh conversation; latency in seconds

evidence.claim: The LLM judge was validated against an independent human panel on a stratified sample of 800 answers (100 per condition): human-panel Fleiss kappa 0.81 [0.78, 0.84] (three raters, 88.5% exact agreement); human-vs-judge Cohen kappa 0.74 pooled (Semantic conditions 0.78, Deep conditions 0.69); numeric score Pearson r 0.83, Spearman rho 0.81, mean absolute difference 5.2 score points.
evidence.value: Human-vs-judge Cohen kappa 0.74; Pearson r 0.83; MAD 5.2 points
evidence.condition: 800 stratified answers; judge agreement lower on Deep conditions (MAD 6.8) than Semantic (MAD 4.1)

facts.evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a), open-ended questions over whole Python repositories; each question answered in a fresh thread with only the target repository available. Four LLMs: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B. Two architectures: ReAct agent (LangChain) with three tools (repo-structure lookup, vector-index retrieval, file reader), vector index built once per repo via chunking+embedding; and Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework) with planning, virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation. Grading by LLM judge cross-validated against a human panel. Failure taxonomy inter-coder agreement: two authors on 400 failures, Cohen kappa 0.86 (symptom) and 0.78 (mechanism), consensus-vs-automatic coding 0.82.
facts.limitations: Scope is read-only repository question answering over repositories that can be indexed; results do not cover code modification, patching, or SWE-Bench-style edit tasks, and the abstract explicitly restricts the conclusion to 'read-only questions over a repository that can be indexed.' The accuracy advantage is consistent in direction across all four models but modest in magnitude for the Gemini 2.5 pair (Cliff's delta ~0.14) and large only for Gemini 3 Flash; part of the large Gemini 3 Flash Pass-rate gap (49.6pp from a 30.9-point score difference) reflects the fixed Pass cutoff rather than the underlying score scale. The two architectures have non-identical action spaces (different tools), which the authors treat as intrinsic to the paradigms rather than a confound but which limits controlled attribution. Judge agreement is lower on Deep conditions (Cohen kappa 0.69, MAD 6.8) than Semantic (0.78, MAD 4.1). The coordination-breakdown failure is partly definitional because only a hierarchical agent can produce it.
facts.project_relevance: Directly informs the agent-acceleration question of whether repository indexing truly lowers end-to-end task cost: for read-only repo QA, a prebuilt vector index is both more accurate and roughly half the cost per correct answer than delegating exploration to an isolated subagent. It also supplies the failure-mode evidence the topic asks about for tool-call delegation correctness risks, quantifying that the largest failure source of the hierarchical design (41.8%) is the planner-subagent hand-off, often producing silently wrong answers. The latency data is a genuine counterpoint (Deep is faster for some models) and means cost/accuracy and latency can diverge, so an indexing shortcut is not automatically the lowest-latency option. Applicability is bounded to read-only QA on indexable repos and should not be extrapolated to patching or editing workflows without separate evidence.
source_notes: Primary source: arXiv 2608.01507v1 (fetched, FETCHED). Evidence Pack covers PDF Pages 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 15, 26 (abstract, intro, background, related work Table 1, experimental design 4/4.1, master comparison Table 3, judge-validity Table 2, failure taxonomy 6.2-6.3).
The pooled 65.2% vs 46.2% headline in the abstract is reproduced as the mean of the four per-model Pass rates in Table 3, so it is treated as a verified figure rather than an unverified claim.
Cost column in Table 3 includes reasoning tokens billed at the completion rate, so it is not the product of the in/out token columns and list prices.

facts.title: ExpertPlex: A High-Goodput Disaggregated Serving System for MoE LLMs with Adaptive Persistent Kernels
facts.event_hint: New MoE LLM serving system (ExpertPlex) that shares experts across prefill/decode while disaggregating attention, with adaptive persistent kernels and attention-initiated MoE communication.
facts.problem: Instance-level prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) for MoE LLMs isolates phases on separate full-model replicas; as MoE weights grow each instance spans tens to hundreds of GPUs, so configured P:D ratios mismatch demand (overprovisioning one phase, overloading the other). Prefill-decode colocation avoids duplication, but Green Context-style spatial partitioning fixes per-kernel phase resources and cannot track resource changes across operations or layerwise variation in routed expert load, causing head-of-line blocking or idle reserved resource bubbles; partitioning every GPU also widens parallelism/communication and lets prefill+decode traffic interfere on the shared network.
facts.mechanism: ExpertPlex shares massive MoE experts across phases while disaggregating lightweight attention modules to the MoE-attention boundary. Three mechanisms: (1) adaptive persistent kernels (APK) that schedule dynamic expert computation at tile granularity for efficient, isolated execution with tile-boundary preemption (no checkpoint/restore/recompute); (2) attention-initiated MoE communication to avoid cross-phase network interference and enable cross-phase communication-computation overlap; (3) a tile-to-cluster model to optimize the mechanisms for maximum goodput. Expert sharing eliminates over 95% of duplicate model weights and multiplexes dynamically sparse expert computation.

evidence.claim: Expert sharing eliminates over 95% of duplicate model weights by sharing MoE experts across prefill and decode phases.
evidence.condition: MoE experts shared across phases while attention is disaggregated; conceptual claim from abstract

evidence.claim: ExpertPlex improves goodput by up to 2.01x over instance-level prefill-decode disaggregation and up to 1.66x over prefill-decode colocation across MiniMax-M2.7 and GLM-5.1-FP8 workloads.
evidence.condition: Serving MiniMax-M2.7 and GLM-5.1-FP8 on NVIDIA H800 nodes; headline abstract claim. Per-setting breakdown now visible: the 1.66x traces to GLM-5.1-FP8/LooGLE over SGLang-PDMux (Section 7.2, PDF Page 11).

evidence.claim: On MiniMax-M2.7 / ShareGPT under the joint TTFT (1s) and TPOT (50ms) SLO, ExpertPlex reaches 11.3 requests/s/node P90 goodput: 2.01x over SGLang-PDD, 2.72x over SGLang-Colocated, 5.65x over SGLang-ChunkedPrefill, and 1.41x over SGLang-PDMux.
evidence.condition: MiniMax-M2.7, ShareGPT, P90 goodput (joint TTFT 1s + TPOT 50ms), H800

evidence.claim: Under tuned GEMM/data-processing tiles, all MiniMax-M2.7 MoE operations have preemption intervals below 25.3 us and GEMM intervals below 10.7 us; the interval depends on tile execution time not token count, allowing a short decode op to preempt a prefill request with thousands of input tokens. REEF's best reported delay is 35 us and requires recomputing the preempted kernel (reference points only).
evidence.baseline: REEF best 35 us (reference); LithOS 250 us, Bless 700 us, GPreempt 100 us (reference points, not MoE-targeted)
evidence.condition: MiniMax-M2.7, tuned tiles; comparison baselines do not target MoE workloads
evidence.source_locator: Section 7.6 Analysis of Preemption Intervals / Figure 15, PDF Page 12

evidence.claim: For GLM-5.1-FP8 (multi-node), ExpertPlex improves goodput by 3.3x over SGLang-ChunkedPrefill on ShareGPT and 5.0x on LooGLE, by 1.5x over SGLang-Colocated on ShareGPT and 2.5x on LooGLE, and by 1.66x over SGLang-PDMux on LooGLE (the source of the abstract's 1.66x headline). On ShareGPT, ExpertPlex and SGLang-PDMux achieve similar joint goodput of about 1.5 req/s/node; on LooGLE, ExpertPlex improves over SGLang-PDMux by 1.66x because long requests expose network interference and Green Context's inability to maximize GPU utilization while preserving TPOT. For MiniMax-M2.7 LooGLE, ExpertPlex improves goodput by 4.12x over SGLang-ChunkedPrefill and by 1.28x over SGLang-PDMux.
evidence.condition: GLM-5.1-FP8 multi-node and MiniMax-M2.7 single-node; ShareGPT and LooGLE workloads; P90 goodput

facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: single-node = one NVIDIA H800 node with 8 GPUs via NVLink; multi-node = up to 3 machines, each 8 H800 GPUs via NVLink, machines linked by 8x 200 Gbps InfiniBand NICs per node. Throughput reported as requests/s/node. Main metric: P90 goodput (highest arrival rate with >=90% of requests meeting both TTFT and TPOT SLOs). Models: MiniMax-M2.7 (1P1D under PDD) and GLM-5.1-FP8. Workloads: ShareGPT (short) and LooGLE (long), Poisson arrivals. SLOs per model/workload (e.g. MiniMax-M2.7 ShareGPT TTFT 1s/TPOT 50ms; LooGLE TTFT 10s/TPOT 100ms; GLM-5.1-FP8 ShareGPT TTFT 2s/TPOT 100ms). Baselines all SGLang-based: SGLang-Colocated, SGLang-ChunkedPrefill, SGLang-PDD, SGLang-PDMux (MuxWise/Green Context, modified for MoE).
facts.limitations: GLM-5.1-FP8 runs out of memory under the 1P1D PDD layout on 24 GPUs, so GLM-5.1-FP8 PDD numbers are not reported. Several baselines cannot express ExpertPlex's 24-GPU fine-grained layout under their parallelism constraints; for GLM-5.1-FP8 those baselines run on the largest compatible 16-GPU layout and are compared via request rates per node. SGLang-PDMux is compatible only with tensor-parallel attention. Multi-node evaluation limited to up to 3 machines. Preemption-interval comparison baselines (LithOS, Bless, GPreempt, PipeSwitch, REEF) are reference points only since they do not target MoE LLM workloads and lack modern MoE kernel features (TMA multicast, CTA clusters, warp specialization, CUDA Graph).
facts.project_relevance: ExpertPlex disaggregates attention by phase while sharing MoE experts, and its attention-initiated MoE communication is a phase-aware network mechanism that isolates prefill vs decode traffic and enables cross-phase communication-computation overlap to avoid network interference. This is directly relevant to the TPN topic's questions about whether serving-network mechanisms can perceive the inference phase and KV-cache position and whether network-side traffic isolation reduces cross-phase interference. However, ExpertPlex's contribution sits at MoE-dispatch/attention disaggregation within an LLM serving cluster rather than being a general Token Performance Network, and the paper reports TTFT/TPOT-goodput and per-node throughput rather than isolated network-utilization or cross-node KV-cache-transfer metrics. (Project inference, separate from source facts.)
source_notes: Primary source: arXiv 2607.18002v2, FETCHED (raw_fulltext_cache_hit=true). Evidence pack is balanced-evidence-v2 front selection (17869 of 72402 chars, 0.7532 reduction).
Authors: Bingyang Wu, Chao Jin, Zili Zhang, Xinming Wei, Yinmin Zhong, Ruidong Zhu (Peking University); Chengxu Yang, Xin Jin, Yuliang Liu (Independent Researcher).

Supplement (PDF Pages 5, 9, 11) provided per-setting goodput multipliers for GLM-5.1-FP8 and LooGLE, resolving the prior evidence gap. The abstract's 1.66x headline traces to GLM-5.1-FP8/LooGLE over SGLang-PDMux.

Table 1 (PDF Page 5) compares ExpertPlex with API Interception, CUDA streams, NVIDIA MPS, Green Context, and NVIDIA MIG on CUDA Graph compatibility, temporal/spatial multiplexing, bounded fast preemption, and bounded fast reallocation.

facts.title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
facts.event_hint: Harness Handbook + BGPD: a behavior-centric handbook for agent harnesses improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality with fewer planner tokens.
facts.problem: Behavior localization is a central bottleneck in evolving production agent harnesses: a modification request describes what behavior should change, but the repository is organized by files/functions/modules, while a single behavior is distributed across many nonadjacent sites spanning execution stages and shared state. Existing code search, repository maps, summarization, and long-context editing make code easier to inspect but still leave developers/agents to recover the behavior-to-code mapping by hand, and agents with limited context may overlook scattered or rarely executed paths.
facts.mechanism: Harness Handbook is a behavior-centric representation built automatically in three phases (Algorithm 2, Appendix A): Phase I deterministic static fact extraction (language adapters parse functions, boundaries, signatures, call edges; unresolved calls are written to an audit log rather than assigned guessed targets; no LLM calls); Phase II behavioral organization maps source units onto an execution-stage skeleton using either function-as-leaf (starts from a trusted seed skeleton S0; budgeted stage and membership review, then region/ordering finalization) or file-as-leaf (describes files first and infers the skeleton; optional refinement) modes; Phase III hierarchical synthesis produces an L1-L3 document tree plus cross-stage state registers, with each entry linked to a statically identified source location. Phase III validates every L3 locator against the current repository and freezes entries that cannot be revalidated (excluding them from localization until refreshed), keeping the repository authoritative for implementation details. The packaged handbook retains a machine-readable synchronization state K_g (program graph, stage skeleton, mode-specific organization state, construction config Theta including organization/generation/register-extraction budgets, and generation cache; seed skeleton S0 retained only in function mode). Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) guides agents from high-level behaviors down to implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source; an automatic resynchronization step updates the handbook on repository change, limiting model calls to four semantic steps (classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, description revision).

evidence.claim: Handbook-Assisted planning raises overall win rates vs Baseline by 10.0 percentage points on Codex and 18.9 points on Terminus-2.
evidence.condition: 30 modification requests per harness; two harnesses (Codex Rust file-as-leaf, Terminus-2 Python function-as-leaf); Handbook-Assisted BGPD vs Baseline arms

evidence.claim: Planner token use falls by 12.7% on Codex and 8.6% on Terminus-2 with handbook assistance.
evidence.condition: Same planning tasks on the two evaluated harnesses

evidence.claim: With handbook guidance a weaker planner matches stronger reference models on Terminus-2: file-level F1 84.7% and 89.3%, symbol-level F1 77.1% and 89.3% against Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references; precision reaches 93.3% against GPT-5.5 at both granularities.
evidence.value: File F1 84.7/89.3, symbol F1 77.1/89.3; precision 93.3% vs GPT-5.5
evidence.condition: Terminus-2; weaker planner + handbook; all 24 file/symbol Recall/Precision/F1 comparisons improved against two independent references
evidence.source_locator: Section 4.2 and Section 5 Conclusion, PDF Page 10

evidence.claim: Complete localization failures (Wrong = zero overlap vs reference) never increase with the handbook and fall by as much as 25.9 points.
evidence.value: up to 25.9 points reduction in Wrong rate

evidence.claim: All six harness-by-type win-rate comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains of 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points; cross-file requests improve 16.3 and 20.0 points; Codex gains most on Query requests (+26.7) and Terminus-2 most on Search-Hostile requests (+33.3).
evidence.condition: Stratified by request type and localization difficulty across the two harnesses

facts.evaluation_context: Two open-source agent harnesses differing by roughly two orders of magnitude: Terminus-2 (Python terminal agent from the Harbor framework, observe-decide-act loop over tmux; 6 source files, 103 internal-function nodes, 41 boundary nodes, 257 resolved call edges; function-as-leaf; built handbook has 20 L2 stages, 106 L3 entries, 10 state registers) and Codex (Rust monorepo behind the Codex coding agent; 2,267 files, 34,363 internal-function nodes, 4,016 boundary nodes, 159,960 resolved call edges; file-as-leaf; 140 L2 stages, 2,267 L3 entries, 62 state registers). 30 modification requests per harness balanced across request type and localization difficulty; two arms (Baseline vs Handbook-Assisted BGPD) with every factor other than handbook access held fixed; reference localization plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. Construction (Appendix A): Phase I is fully deterministic with no LLM; Phase II and Phase III are budgeted (organization/generation/register-extraction budgets recorded in config Theta) but the actual construction token/time cost and a net build-plus-resync cost-benefit are not reported.
facts.limitations: Validated on only two harnesses (though they differ sharply in scale and language). Static analysis is conservative: unresolved calls are logged rather than assigned guessed targets, and content that cannot be parsed/classified is frozen or recorded in the coverage record; Phase III freezes any L3 locator that cannot be revalidated against the current repository. The specific weaker planner model whose F1/precision are reported is still not named in the visible evidence. The initial Handbook construction cost (Phase I-III) in tokens/model calls/time and a net build-plus-resynchronization cost-benefit are not quantified; only the qualitative fact that Phase I uses no LLM and that Phase II/III run under recorded budgets is available. Gain variation is not fully explained by labeled difficulty. The paper reports planning/localization quality and planner-token cost, not end-to-end executed task success rate or wall-clock latency.
facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses the Agent语义加速 question of cutting repeated Read/Grep/context localization: a behavior-centric index lets an agent navigate from a requested behavior to source sites instead of iteratively exploring files, and it reports exactly the metrics the topic values (planner-token reduction of 12.7%/8.6% and localization F1/Precision). Caveat for project inference: it measures edit-plan/localization quality, not end-to-end task latency or success rate, and build/resync cost is only partly quantified (Phase I is LLM-free but Phase II/III budgets and totals are not reported); net benefit and applicability to general (non-harness) code search still need confirmation.
source_notes: Primary arXiv PDF (2607.13285v1) fetched; evidence pack covers abstract, intro, representation (Page 4), construction pipeline (Page 5), construction details Appendix A (Pages 14, 17), experiment setup (Pages 7, 19) and results/conclusion (Page 10).
Headline win-rate and token numbers carry explicit baseline, two-harness condition, and section locators.

Appendix A / Algorithm 2 (PDF Page 14): Phase I BuildGraph deterministic no-LLM; Phase II function-as-leaf (seed skeleton S0 + budgeted review) vs file-as-leaf (cards + stage inference, optional refinement); Phase III Synthesize + ValidateAndFreezeLocators + RenderAndPackage. Sync state K_g retains graph, skeleton, org state, config Theta (incl. budgets), cache (PDF Page 17).
Weaker-planner identity, construction cost (tokens/time/net cost-benefit), and any end-to-end latency/success metrics are not visible and remain as gaps.

evidence_gaps.question: Which specific planner model is the weaker planner whose F1/precision are reported against the Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references, and is it the same across both harnesses?
What is the initial Handbook construction cost (Phase I-III) in tokens/model calls/time, and does the paper report a net cost-benefit including build plus resynchronization?
Does the paper report any downstream end-to-end task success rate or wall-clock latency from executing the Handbook-Assisted plans, beyond plan-quality and planner-token metrics?
